rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at moderate temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the overall elution window and any late hold-eluters. The wide composition range and mid-length gradient give a good first estimate of which parts of the gradient need trimming and whether retention is dominated by window, slope, or temperature.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only lever is shortening t_last below 10 min while keeping the last peak inside the gradient. The first run suggests the elution window is roughly phi_e 0.11 to 0.41, so trimming to a narrower, steeper window should keep separation adequate and pull the last peak earlier.

We only need to shave about 0.6 min off the last peak, and the current worst pair still has margin, so a slightly steeper gradient plus a small temperature increase should bring t_last under 10 min. This also tests whether the close mid-cluster pair is temperature-sensitive enough to remain fully resolved while gaining speed.

The collapse of pair 6/7 at higher temperature shows this pair is strongly temperature-sensitive, so revert to 40 C while keeping the shorter gradient that already got the run comfortably under 10 min. This isolates whether tG 8 at the original selectivity is enough to preserve full resolution and improve on injection 2.

The critical pair 6/7 worsened when the gradient got steeper, so keep tG and temperature fixed but narrow the high-organic end to make the gradient shallower in the region where all peaks elute. The observed elution window is still well below 0.55, so this should improve the mid-cluster resolution without pushing the last peak past 10 min.

We are very close to the optimum, with only a tiny shortfall from pair 6/7 and a small time penalty; lowering temperature should strengthen selectivity for that critical pair, which previously degraded sharply when temperature increased. This tests whether a modest cooling can push the worst pair to at least 1.5 while keeping t_last near 10 min.

Temperature changes hurt selectivity, so return to 40 C and make the gradient slightly shallower to recover full resolution around the critical mid-cluster while staying in the already well-targeted phi window. Based on injections 2 and 5, this should lift the 6/7 pair above 1.5 with only a small increase in t_last, potentially reaching the score maximum of 1.000 if the last peak stays at or below 10 min.

The best run is limited by a nearly resolved 6/7 pair and a tiny time penalty; since lowering T in the narrower window shifted the problematic adjacency from 6/7 to 5/6, reopen the window slightly at the high end while keeping the fast 8 min gradient. This tests whether a small increase in phi1 can pull the last peak back under 10 min yet let the altered selectivity at 35 C keep all adjacent pairs at or above 1.5.

The data indicate 35 C makes the 5/6 pair collapse and 45 C makes the 6/7 pair collapse, but the narrower phi1=0.55 window improved the critical spacing at 40 C. Testing the same narrow window at 45 C will map whether the selectivity tradeoff is monotonic and help bracket the true optimum near 40 C, while still keeping the run short.

At 40 C the only remaining deficit is a very small shortfall in the 6/7 pair, and narrowing phi1 from 0.60 to 0.55 improved that pair substantially; pushing one more step to 0.50 should further shallow the gradient in the active elution region. The tradeoff is some extra retention of the last peak, but because the gain needed in resolution is tiny, this is the most direct shot at reaching full resolution with minimal method change.

The best method is very close, and changing phi1 or temperature too much causes either time or selectivity problems; lowering phi0 one step is a gentler way to slightly reduce gradient steepness and potentially separate the critical mid pair without strongly affecting the late peak. This also avoids the large t_last penalty seen when phi1 was cut to 0.50.

The best point remains 0.10/0.55/8 at 40 C, and the temperature sensitivity appears highly nonlinear: 35 C hurt by changing the critical adjacency, while 45 C strongly collapsed 6/7. Testing 30 C deliberately probes the lower side more strongly to see whether a different selectivity regime can fully resolve all pairs despite some retention increase, which could still improve CRF if the worst pair gains enough.

A shorter gradient at the same 40 C and optimized phi window directly tests whether the tiny remaining deficit is best traded for a faster last peak; if 6/7 only drops slightly, eliminating the time penalty could surpass the current best. This is the most informative unexplored point adjacent to the current optimum in the tG dimension.

Comparing 8 and 10 min at 0.10/0.60 showed the critical pair still has some margin at the wider window, so a 6 min run there could give a better speed/selectivity balance than 0.10/0.55/6, which over-compressed 6/7. This explores the last untested neighboring point around the apparent optimum in the tG–phi1 space.

The unresolved pair responds mainly to gradient shape near its elution zone, while dropping phi0 to 0.05 made retention longer without helping enough; raising phi0 to 0.15 should trim early low-organic time and slightly redistribute the gradient over the active region. This is a targeted check for whether starting closer to the first peak can keep the last peak at or below 10 min while nudging the critical pair to full resolution.

You have already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000, so the best practical use of another injection is to see whether the same selectivity can be preserved in a faster method. This keeps the newly successful phi window and temperature but steepens the gradient to test if full credit can be retained with a shorter cycle time.

Since 0.15/0.55/8/40 already achieves the maximum score, the only worthwhile exploration is whether a slightly higher starting organic can keep all pairs at full resolution while pulling the last peak just below 10.0 min. This tests whether further trimming the low-organic portion preserves the successful selectivity pattern better than shortening tG did.

You already have the maximum CRF, so the best remaining question is whether the successful trend with higher phi0 can further shorten t_last while still keeping the critical 6/7 pair at or above 1.5. This is the nearest unexplored step from the current optimum and directly tests the robustness margin before early peaks become too compressed.

The jump to phi0=0.25 over-compressed the front end, so phi0=0.20 appears to be the upper safe limit; now increasing phi1 one step tests whether the last peak can be pulled earlier while preserving the just-adequate 6/7 resolution and avoiding the new 1/2 problem. This is a direct robustness check around the two score-maximizing methods already found.

The two perfect methods suggest the optimum lies on a ridge where increasing phi0 compensates for a narrower window, so 0.15/0.60 is the missing intermediate point between the known winners and the wider faster but slightly under-resolved 0.20/0.60 condition. This tests whether that tradeoff can preserve full resolution while shortening the run relative to 0.15/0.55.

Both 0.15/0.55 and 0.20/0.55 give perfect scores, so the next useful boundary test is whether keeping phi0 at the faster successful value but narrowing the window one step can preserve the critical 6/7 resolution while holding the last peak under 10 min. This maps the lower-phi1 edge of the optimum region without revisiting already weak temperature or tG directions.

The perfect region is now well bracketed, and 0.20/0.50 showed that lowering phi1 too far mainly hurts by delaying the last peak rather than losing resolution. Testing 0.15/0.50 maps the remaining corner of that region to confirm the optimum window boundary and provide a robustness check around the two score-maximizing methods.

You already have a perfect method, so the remaining value is robustness mapping near the optimum. Extending tG one step at the faster perfect composition tests whether the 6/7 margin can be increased further while staying under the 10 min threshold, which would identify a more forgiving operating point if it still scores 1.000.

With the maximum score already achieved, the last few injections are best used to probe robustness to temperature around a winning composition. This checks whether the broader-resolution winner at phi0 0.15 tolerates higher temperature any better than the phi0 0.10 case, potentially revealing whether the optimum ridge is composition-stabilized or strictly tied to 40 C.

For the final injection, probe the lower-temperature robustness of the faster perfect method, since 45 C clearly collapses the critical pair and only 35 C at lower phi0 was tested before. This will show whether the phi0=0.20 winner is uniquely stable at 40 C or whether its selectivity window broadens on the low-temperature side.
